item.title: AI-assisted Proofs Come with Additional Responsibilities
item.content:encoded:
Recently, Marcin Polkowski announced popso: a vibe coded MILP solver. He advertised it as 'written from scratch' and 'already solving more problems than HiGHS and SCIP'. On the process, all he writes is this:

Does anyone know how long it takes to write a competitive MILP solver? [...] The textbook answer is "a team, about a decade". My answer, as of this week, is "hold my Coke Zero".

Despite being reductive, I do like this question.

popso is not a well-executed project. For one, it is clearly tuned on the test set. Performance variability[1] in MIP is high, and so tuning on your test set is problematic. Much of that variability is within families. That is, when you write an instance generator and you tune on one set of samples, then even if you draw fresh samples from those generators you are still overtuned. This invalidates all Polkowski's benchmark results.

Benjamin Müller of COPT additionally pointed out various parts of the code come from HiGHS and SCIP, and that 'one could be tempted to say that the AI just created a combination of the two solvers'. Indeed, Claude's comments in the code reveal that the other solvers were used as a direct reference.

So far, this is a story like so many others. An LLM creates a large piece of bad work. The machine operator fails the basic responsibilities that we have towards each other. Not meaningfully different from what OpenAI and Anthropic have been doing.

But not all LLM-involved projects hit the same failures. I have seen plenty of non-examples. Colleagues who prompted to solve mathematical problems within their expertise and wrote up the result as a well-readable paper with adequate exposition and citations. These are pieces of work that, had they been produced last year, I would have called 'nice' or even 'good'. Nevertheless, I do think many of these papers fail their responsibilities. Specifically: they fail their specific responsibilities as LLM-involved projects.

We must not forget: these papers required a different (and less) work from their authors. A significant chunk of the work was performed by the machine, with the authors taking up roles as machine operators. This is a methodological novelty.

In other fields of science, papers report their methodology. Mathematicians have not traditionally needed to do so, because every paper's methods were the same. You read the literature, walk through a forest, discuss at the whiteboard, and take a long shower. At some point you have a strategy, and then you spend however long working it out and writing it up.

Now we have more options in terms of different methods. That means we need more substantive methodological reporting. The 'AI disclosures' that people are writing are far too meagre. It is not enough to say "GPT-6 pro was used to prove Lemma 1, 2, and 3". That is distributing credit, not a description of methods.[2] The methods section needs to be a full section of the paper, able to cover a page with little issue.

When you study an object, you always study the method as well. You cannot learn about the planets without learning about your telescope, and you cannot study medicines without learning about mice. Similarly, I don't think we can learn about math from LLMs without learning about the LLMs. That means the specific usage of the LLMs must be reported in papers.

Here are just a few examples of things that I would like to see reported:

  1. We tested LLMs A, B, and C. Each was prompted n times for this problem, and respectively x%, y% and z% of sessions outputted the key ideas that were needed for this theorem.

  2. We used a $N/month subscription from vendor D over the course of M days. The session used K tokens and, if one were to pay API prices for that, would have cost $L.

  3. We prompted the machine with the problem like this, after a while we suggested such-and-so strategy and told it to look at these papers for ideas.

  4. When we asked the robot post-hoc to identify where the ideas came from, it said UVW99. This answer was true/false.

  5. The machine gave extraneous details O, P, Q, and left out important steps R, S, T.

  6. All raw chat transcripts.

What unifies these example questions is that they can only be answered by the original machine operators. Some are about how the operator used the machine, others have been could be prompted by anyone but became impossible once the paper was publically available and assimilated into the borg.

Reporting on your machine use is very common in other computational fields. I often hear people say that writing computational MIP papers consists of much more effort writing than effort in computation. That is because they (or their reviewers..) know that methodological transparency is valuable. It is just as important a piece of the science as the actual results. The change I ask for has long been normal in other fields.

Let's wrap back to Polkowski. Not only is it not good, he is missing out on answering all the methodological questions that came across him. Most visibly, 'how long does it take to write a competitive MILP solver?'. He is aware of the question, asks it himself, but refuses to attempt a serious answer. That makes his effort a waste of everyone's attention.

I want to highlight one positive example. After 3SUM, Josh Alman and Virginia Vassilevska Williams each provided an examplary amount of information. This is key scientific information, and I would have loved to see it all included in the paper. Skipping that is a missed opportunity, and I believe that going forward we should start demanding papers to include a substantial section of this exact nature.

[1] Performance variability is the phenomenon where small changes in the code can cause a lot of variation in running time. A change which improves your geometric mean time by 1% may increase the running time on some instances by 2-3x and decrease others by 0.5x. These changes can be algorithmic, but can also come from changing the random seed or permuting the rows and columns of a model.
[2] The STOC 2027 CFP is one example of a document that is confused about this difference. The CFP mandates 'disclose of substantive use' but the template they provide reads 'AI methodology: We used [Tool Name] to assist with [Brief Description of Use]. The tool materially affected [Sections X and Y]. More details can be found in [Section Z]. The authors verified the correctness and originality of all content, including references.' This is merely a disclosure of usage but it is titled as methodology.

item.title: The New Hiring/Job Search Meta
item.content:encoded:
Many colleagues are struggling with The Hiring Question.

For junior folks, The Hiring Question is "what should I do to get a job in the LLM-era." They worry whether they should get in on the roboticized proofs gold rush, and how this interacts with the fear of getting scooped. There is much uncertainty about how journals or hiring committees would value their work, if the committee knew that the applicant didn't come up with their own proofs.

For senior folks, The Hiring Question is the opposite side of this coin. They are unsure how to define research excellence for their institution, leading to uncertainty about how to evaluate candidates. Advisors are also unsure how to help their students.

I am here to tell you, that Europe has solved all these problems. The next meta[1] has already been invented, and once American institutions catch up to this strategy then the career game theory will work itself out to a comfortable place for everyone.

Three Papers

Every respectable institution knows that bibliometrics are cringe. Research assesment cannot be based on counting somebody's number of papers, nor can it be based on seeing which journal or conference those papers appeared in. This is a broadly supported norm, even if some people still struggle. When I have been on hiring committees, there was always some laggard still counting papers and looking at CORE rankings. But when you remind them of the institution's commitment to DORA, these people are quickly embarrassed into silence.

What do we do instead? Every job applicant is asked to attach 3 papers to their application. Often these will be their 3 most prominent papers, though they can also select a subset that best conveys their breadth of work. In any case, these will be 3 papers that the applicant is proud of. These 3 papers are in addition to a CV (including publication list) and research statement.

The committee will look at the attached papers to evaluate the quality of the candidate's past work, and look at the research statement to estimate the quality of their future work. The role of the full publication list is merely to support the case that the candidate has the required experience to credibly execute on their promised future plans.

The Meta for Institutions

This phenomenon, of a limited number of papers considered for evaluation, is widespread but not universal. In the UK this principle is part of the national evaluation of universities. Both the German granting agency DFG and the Dutch NWO evaluate a candidate's track record based on the few publications they may attach (Europe's ERC counts all the way up to 10). Every hiring committee I have been on has followed the same 3 paper format, but only 1 or 2 jobs that I have applied to did.

We see that the '3 papers only' principle is nowhere near universal. But it is common enough that it shapes your career strategy as an early career researcher. If, as an applicant, you want to have a shot at getting these jobs or grants, then all you care about is your top 3 papers. That is because papers 4 up through infinity do not count.

For institutions, following this evaluation meta allows you to hire responsible researchers at the top of their field. Those backwards institutions who still count papers and venues become less attractive places to work, because nobody wants to live under the leadership of bean counters. Such institutions get a bad reputation and are left to hire the salami-slicers among the talent pool.

The Meta for Applicants

If you have only 3 papers to show off your skills as a researcher, it would be bad strategy to use 1 of those slots on your ChatGPT weekend project. A paper like that neither demonstrates your capabilities, nor does it illustrate what you spend your time on.

A good paper, one which increases your chances of getting hired, is one that represents a large fraction of your research time, reflects your standard of work, and conveys which subjects you consider interesting enough to spend effort on. In your research statement, you describe what type of work you have done, what you value, and what you plan to do. Your three papers you choose to best support your story.

It is up to the hiring committee to then look at everyone's stories, including the implicit or explicit messages about LLM use, and select applicants based on the committee's priorities. That is where pluralism reigns: there are no priorities that all scientists or all committees would agree. As Feyerabend would say, 'anything goes.' Focus on presenting yourself in a way that you are proud of, and by applying to jobs you will eventually find employment and colleagues that mesh with how you approach mathematical work.

Why is This Good?

In the age of robots, the European meta is more desireable than ever before. The game theory for junior researchers is clear: any time you spend effort on a new paper, it should at least beat your 3rd best ever paper in quality. This encourages slow science and careful work, discouraging minimum-publishable-units and other degrading practices.

Under the three-paper meta there is no incentive to post flag-staking AI slop, even when you fear you may get scooped if you wait. You cannot attach slop to your application, because the hiring committee will actually look at your attached papers.

The three-paper meta has been favored for years already at all respectable institutions. In today's mathematically uncertain times these hiring strategies are more desireable than ever before.

Conclusion

The three-paper meta already exists, it is prevalent enough that young researchers can build their careers on this. I personally did so. I publish ~1 paper per year and have never worried about pressure to publish more. That strategy has let me build a body of work that I am proud of, and has also led to stable employment. The same has worked for many of my friends and colleagues.

If we wish to reduce the phenomenon of AI slop flag planting, the main thing we need is for the alternative strategy (publishing lots of low-effort papers) to further lose out for young people. Hence, it is high time for bean-counters to step back and let their deparments enter the 21st century.

[1] In video game culture, the meta refers to the current dominant strategy for playing. Partly the meta is the current Nash equilibirium, partly it is the current state-of-the-art knowledge of optimal play. A game's meta can evolve based on outside circumstances (rules changes, new content being released) or inside circumstances (new strategies are found and disseminated, new counterplay is found).

item.title: Community and Company
item.description: My community is under attack by commercial interests.
item.content:encoded:
My community is under attack by commercial interests. Since last week, speedrun.com refuses to distribute our database of speedrun accomplishments under the agreed-upon Creative Commons license. This licensing dispute is a major breach of trust and an abdication of SRC's responsibilities to the community. Individual game's communities are all scrambling to find a new home for their leaderboards. SRC has the audacity to say its for our own good.

My other community is also under attack by commercial interests. OpenAI and Anthropic are telling their models to solve open mathematical problems, presumably to evaluate their models' capabilities. Sure, if that is productive then I won't judge that. What I do disapprove of, is that OpenAI is yeeting all their exhaust onto the internet.

When you prove a theorem, you are imparted a responsibility to the field. At minimum you need to explain what you did, including which steps required new ideas and which steps are already well-known. More substantively, you are expected to nurture the literature. If an important idea was poorly explained in its first incarnation, then you have to explain it better in your work. These demands are broadly accepted and are not controversial. Any time you meet the demands, the resulting paper is highly appreciated and valued.[1] The responsibility is yours because you have the opportunity to publish a paper on the subject.

OpenAI is doing the exact opposite. They do not care about their 'manuscripts'. They don't bother putting in appropriate attribution of ideas, their work contains errors, and they don't even bother with consistent presentation or formatting. This actively sets back the state of the literature.

Why are they doing this? Is there a benefit to their releasing this exhaust? Does science benefit? OpenAI says these results took 3 hours of LLM time on average with their internal model. Likely their public models can achieve the same outcomes when instructed by expert guidance. That's why they keep scooping their own customers.[2] A scooping that, I will add, is only possible because OpenAI outputs such sloppy work.

If an expert prompts a result, they take up the mantle of responsibility I describe above. OpenAI not only refuses to take their responsibility, but they prevent their own customers from doing so. And they have the audacity to say they do it for the good of science.

[1] One example of such a valued paper is Daniel and I's smoothed analysis paper. Yes we proved better running time bounds, but mostly using ideas that were in the literature already. The contribution of the paper was that it was nice to read, unlike the notoriously opaque literature that came before it. It would have been difficult to justify the time we spent writing this all up nicely if we hadn't also improved the result quantitatively, hence the responsibility. The paper remains my most visible piece of work, still accruing more citations per year than later follow-up work.
[2] Here is one example from today of OpenAI customers who got scooped because they were spending their time writing up a nice paper instead of staking a flag on github dot com.
